props.title: Dangerous Liaisons

sections.content: Dangerous Liaisons (1988) stands as a masterpiece of calculated seduction and social manipulation in pre-revolutionary France. Stephen Frears directs Glenn Close and John Malkovich in career-defining performances as aristocratic schemers wielding sex as a weapon. The film's influence echoes through later period dramas like The Age of Innocence (1993) and Valmont (1989), showing how deadly games of passion destroy lives beneath polite society's veneer. Christopher Hampton's razor-sharp screenplay adapts Choderlos de Laclos' epistolary novel with vicious wit, while James Acheson's Oscar-winning costumes turn fashion into armor.

sections.content: The film's exploration of aristocratic decadence finds powerful echoes in other period pieces that examine moral corruption among the privileged. Barry Lyndon (1975) shares its meticulous attention to 18th-century detail and social climbing, while Amadeus (1984) similarly portrays talent twisted by jealousy and spite. The way Dangerous Liaisons uses letters and written correspondence as weapons prefigures modern films about social manipulation like Notes on a Scandal (2006).

Close's Marquise de Merteuil and Malkovich's Vicomte de Valmont represent a deadly partnership that influenced countless later screen villains. Their sophisticated cruelty can be seen in the dynamics between characters in The Remains of the Day (1993) and Atonement (2007), where unspoken feelings and rigid social codes lead to tragedy. The film's costume design and art direction created a template for how to portray aristocratic decadence, influencing everything from Portrait of a Lady (1996) to Anna Karenina (2012). movies.title: Quills
movies.slug: Geoffrey Rush stars as the Marquis de Sade in this exploration of sexuality and power in 18th century France

sections.content: The film's exploration of gender dynamics remains startlingly relevant. The Marquise's famous speech about women's limited options in society echoes through later feminist period pieces like The Duchess (2008) and Belle (2013). Michelle Pfeiffer's innocent Madame de Tourvel provides the moral center, her genuine emotions contrasting with the calculated games of the main characters. This dynamic influenced later films about sexual manipulation like The Piano Teacher (2001) and Elle (2016).
